q: Heat is the form of energy that can be transferred from one system to another as a result of ____ difference.
e: Heat is energy that flows from a hotter system to a colder one. A temperature difference is the cause, not a mass or volume gap. Match the two temperatures and net heat flow stops.

q: Heat transfer is a discipline of thermal engineering that concerns the generation, use, conversion, and exchange of ____ energy between systems.
e: Heat transfer is the thermal-engineering study of generating, using, converting and exchanging thermal energy. That is a flow problem, not just a balance sheet of U. Thermodynamics sits beside it as the equilibrium partner.

q: Thermodynamics deals with ____ states by outlining the relationship between energy and work.
e: Thermodynamics maps equilibrium states and how energy links to work. It does not track the rate of heat flow through a wall. Heat transfer is the complementary flow subject.

q: One of the basic requirement for heat transfer is the presence of a ____ difference.
e: A temperature difference is the basic requirement for heat transfer. No gap, no net flow. Pressure or mass differences are different driving forces.

q: There can be no net heat transfer between two systems that are at the ____ temperature.
e: Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow.

q: There are three basic ways of heat transfer; namely, heat conduction, heat convection and heat ____.
e: The three heat-transfer modes are conduction, convection and radiation. Conduction is neighbour vibration, convection is bulk fluid motion, radiation is electromagnetic waves. Convection and radiation are the other two modes, with bulk flow or electromagnetic waves.

q: In fluids, heat is mainly transferred by ____, in which the motion of the fluid itself carries heat from one place to another.
e: In fluids the main heat carrier is convection, because the fluid itself moves. Hot, less dense fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks. Conduction in a solid does not need that bulk current.

q: In solid, heat is transferred by ____ process in which heat energy is transferred among the adjacent parts of the material without the motion of the material itself.
e: In a solid, heat travels by conduction. Atoms stay in place and vibrate, handing energy to neighbours. The material as a whole does not flow.

q: The third way to transfer heat energy is by radiation process in the form of ____ waves.
e: Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not attenuate the wave. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not.

q: The individual parts of a medium do not move whole in heat ____.
e: In conduction the bulk of the medium does not move as a whole. Energy is handed along adjacent parts. That is why a metal poker can heat your hand while the rod stays put.

q: Heat energy is transferred by successive distribution among the ____ parts in heat conduction.
e: Conduction hands energy to neighbouring atoms while the bulk stays put. Metals add free electrons on top of those vibrations. Convection and radiation are the other two modes, with bulk flow or electromagnetic waves.

q: When heat is transferred via conduction, heat energy is transferred internally by ____ of atoms and molecules.
e: Conduction hands energy to neighbouring atoms while the bulk stays put. Metals add free electrons on top of those vibrations. Convection and radiation are the other two modes, with bulk flow or electromagnetic waves. A rigid solid can conduct; it cannot convect.

q: Metals have many ____ electrons.
e: Metals and many have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of Metals would describe a different law.

q: Since these free electrons can carry heat, metals are generally very good ____ of heat.
e: Metals have many free electrons. Those electrons can drift and carry thermal energy, so metals are good heat conductors. Bound electrons locked to one ion cannot roam like that.

q: The rate of heat conduction through a material of cross-sectional area A is proportional to the temperature difference $\Delta T$, but is inversely proportional to the ____ $l$ of the material.
e: Heat current through a slab is inversely proportional to thickness l. A thinner wall, larger area, or larger Delta T raises H. Convection and radiation are the other two modes, with bulk flow or electromagnetic waves.

q: where k is the ____ of the material, which is a measure of the ability of a material to conduct heat.
e: Thermal conductivity k measures how readily a material carries heat. SI unit is watt per metre per kelvin. High k is a conductor; low k is an insulator.

q: The ratio $\frac{T_2-T_1}{l}$ is called ____ gradient.
e: Temperature gradient is the temperature drop per unit thickness. Fourier's heat flux is proportional to that gradient. Thickness l sits in the denominator of the conduction rate.

q: This mathematical model of heat conduction was first formulated by the French physicist ____ in his Fourier's law of heat conduction.
e: Fourier wrote the conduction law that heat flux follows the temperature gradient. The French physicist Jean Baptiste Joseph Fourier gave that mathematical model. Convection and radiation are the other two modes, with bulk flow or electromagnetic waves.

q: Negative sign indicates that temperature T must ____ as distance x increases.
e: The minus sign in Fourier's local law says temperature must decrease as distance x increases along the heat flow. Heat runs down the gradient. A plus sign would send heat toward the hot end, which is backwards.

q: The thermal conductivity of a material can be defined as the rate of heat transfer per unit area per unit ____ gradient.
e: Thermal conductivity k measures how readily a material carries heat. SI unit is watt per metre per kelvin. High k is a conductor; low k is an insulator. Temperature gradient is the temperature drop per unit thickness.

q: A high value for thermal conductivity indicates that the material is a good thermal conductor, and a low value indicates that the material is a poor thermal conductor or thermal ____.
e: Low thermal conductivity means a thermal insulator. Rubber, wood and styrofoam are the usual low-k examples. Copper and silver sit at the opposite, high-k, end.

q: Note that materials such as copper and silver that are good ____ conductors are also good heat conductors, and have high values of thermal conductivity.
e: Thermal conductivity k measures how readily a material carries heat. SI unit is watt per metre per kelvin. High k is a conductor; low k is an insulator. Photographic film is a thin layer of silver compounds.

q: Materials such as rubber, wood, and styrofoam are poor conductors of heat and have ____ conductivity values.
e: Rubber, wood and styrofoam are poor heat conductors with low k. They make good thermal insulators. Do not file them next to copper.

q: Heat convection is the flow of heat through a fluid from places of higher temperature to places of lower temperature by movement of the ____ itself.
e: Convection is heat flow through a fluid by movement of the fluid itself, from hotter places to colder places. Buoyancy drives natural convection because hot fluid is less dense. Conduction keeps the bulk still; radiation needs no fluid.

q: In heat convection, the transfer of energy occurs between an object and its environment due to fluid ____.
e: Convection is heat carried by the fluid itself as it circulates. Hot fluid is less dense, so buoyancy lifts it. Conduction keeps the bulk still; radiation needs no fluid.

q: Convection currents are set up in the fluid because the hotter part of the fluid is not as dense as the cooler part, so there is an upward ____ force on the hotter fluid.
e: Hotter fluid is less dense, so an upward buoyant force lifts it while cooler fluid sinks. That cell is a convection current. Conduction keeps the bulk still; radiation needs no fluid.

q: Convection occurs only in a liquid or a gas, never in a ____.
e: Convection is heat carried by the fluid itself as it circulates. Hot fluid is less dense, so buoyancy lifts it. Conduction keeps the bulk still; radiation needs no fluid. That current never starts inside a rigid solid.

q: Buoyant force is what drives ____ convection, where the pressure difference between air heated by heat sources and surrounding ambient air drives the hot air upwards.
e: Hotter fluid is less dense, so an upward buoyant force lifts it while cooler fluid sinks. That cell is a convection current. Conduction keeps the bulk still; radiation needs no fluid. Natural convection is buoyancy-driven; a fan would be forced convection.

q: The basic equation for the rate of convection heat transfer is known as ____ law of cooling.
e: Newton's law of cooling is the basic convection-rate equation, H = q A (T2 - T1). q is the convective coefficient in W m^-2 K^-1. Conduction keeps the bulk still; radiation needs no fluid.

q: where H is the rate of heat convection, q is the convective heat transfer ____.
e: q is the convective heat transfer coefficient. SI unit is W m^-2 K^-1, one extra metre compared with k. Conduction keeps the bulk still; radiation needs no fluid.

q: When $T_2 > T_1$, heat is gained by the object and H is ____.
e: Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow. T 2 T 1 heat is gained cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Heat radiation is a transfer of heat that does not require a ____ medium.
e: Radiation is heat as electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not weaken the wave. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not.

q: Heat is transferred by thermal radiation which are electromagnetic waves that pass through a medium or even ____.
e: Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not attenuate the wave. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not. Mechanical or sound waves are a different family.

q: Unlike conduction and convection, the transfer of energy by radiation does not require an ____ medium.
e: Conduction hands energy to neighbouring atoms while the bulk stays put. Metals add free electrons on top of those vibrations. Convection and radiation are the other two modes, with bulk flow or electromagnetic waves. That current never starts inside a rigid solid.

q: In fact, energy transfer by radiation is the fastest (at the speed of ____) and it suffers no attenuation in a vacuum.
e: Attenuation is loss of wave amplitude along the path. Viscosity sets that damping rate for sound. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not.

q: Thermal radiation is the form of radiation emitted by bodies because of their ____.
e: Thermal radiation is emitted because of a body's temperature. Every body above absolute zero radiates. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not.

q: All bodies at a temperature above ____ zero emit thermal radiation.
e: Radiation is heat as electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not weaken the wave. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not. It travels at the speed of light.

q: Thermal radiation differs from other forms of electromagnetic radiation such as X-rays, gamma rays, microwave and radio wave that are not related to ____.
e: Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not attenuate the wave. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not. Thermal radiation differs from other forms of cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Radiation is mostly considered to be a ____ phenomenon for solids that are opaque to thermal radiation.
e: Radiation is heat as electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not weaken the wave. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not. Radiation is mostly considered to be a cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The object which can absorb all the electromagnetic radiations falling upon it is called a ____.
e: Thermal radiation is electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not attenuate the wave. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not. A blackbody absorbs all electromagnetic radiation that falls on it.

q: The total ____ power is defined as the total radiant energy of different wavelengths emitted from unit area of a surface of a body in one second.
e: Total emissive power is radiant energy of all wavelengths per unit area per second. A blackbody's value grows as T^4. Emissivity then scales a real surface down from that ideal.

q: The total emissive power of a blackbody is directly proportional to the ____ power of absolute temperature.
e: Total emissive power is all wavelengths of radiant energy leaving unit area in one second. For a blackbody it grows as T^4. Real surfaces emit less, scaled by emissivity.

q: The radiation emitted by all real surfaces is ____ than the radiation emitted by a blackbody at the same temperature.
e: Radiation is heat as electromagnetic waves. No material medium is required, and vacuum does not weaken the wave. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not. A blackbody absorbs every electromagnetic wave that hits it and is also the best emitter.

q: Emissivity is defined as the ____ of the total emissive power of an object to that of the blackbody, at the same temperature and wavelength.
e: Total emissive power is all wavelengths of radiant energy leaving unit area in one second. For a blackbody it grows as T^4. Real surfaces emit less, scaled by emissivity. Shininess drops that ratio.

q: Emissivity of an object depends to a large extent on how ____ it is.
e: Emissivity is emitted power over blackbody power at the same T and wavelength. Shininess drops the ratio toward zero. A dull black surface sits near 1.

q: A black object is a good absorber and a good radiator whose emissivity is close to ____.
e: A black object is a good absorber and a good radiator, so emissivity is close to 1. White, clear, or silver-coated surfaces sit near 0. Good absorber and good emitter travel together.

q: Note that the emissivity of an object depends on the ____ of radiation.
e: Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating. Longer lambda, larger angle in d sin theta = m lambda, so red sits farther out than violet. Conduction and convection both need matter; this path does not.

q: The net energy change is simply the difference between the radiated energy and the ____ energy.
e: Net energy change of a radiating body is radiated energy minus absorbed energy. A body in a hotter room absorbs more than it emits and warms up. In a colder room it is a net emitter.

q: Thermodynamics is the study of systems involving energy in the form of heat and ____.
e: Thermodynamics studies systems whose energy appears as heat and work. A piston confining gas in a cylinder is the usual picture. Mechanical kinetic energy alone is not the whole subject.

q: A good example of a thermodynamic system is gas confined by a ____ in a cylinder.
e: A gas trapped by a piston in a cylinder is a clean thermodynamic system. You can add heat, do work, and track U. Valves and springs may appear in engines, but the textbook starter is the piston.

q: Thermal ____ is an important concept in thermodynamics.
e: Thermal equilibrium means the same temperature and no net heat flow. Zeroth law lets that shared temperature be compared. A maximum heat current would require a temperature gap.

q: When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, there is no net ____ transfer between them.
e: Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer, which happens when temperatures match. Zeroth law then lets a thermometer define that shared temperature. Maximum heat flow would mean the opposite, a temperature gap.

q: The ____ law of thermodynamics is a simple definition of thermodynamic equilibrium.
e: Zeroth law: if A and B each equilibrate with C, then A equilibrates with B. That shared equilibrium is what a thermometer reads as temperature. A fourth body is not in the statement.

q: It states that: When two objects are separately in thermodynamic equilibrium with a ____ object, they all are in thermodynamic equilibrium with each other.
e: Thermal equilibrium means the same temperature and no net heat flow. Zeroth law lets that shared temperature be compared. A maximum heat current would require a temperature gap. States that When two objects are separately cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The first law of thermodynamics is an application of the conservation ____ for heat and thermodynamic processes.
e: First law is conservation of energy applied to heat and thermodynamic processes. Delta U = Q - W, with W the work done by the system. Momentum or mass conservation is a different book.

q: The first law of thermodynamics relates the change in ____ energy of a system to heat added and the work done by the system.
e: Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy of the particles. For an ideal gas it depends only on absolute temperature. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work.

q: The change in internal energy U of a system is equal to the net heat flow Q into the system minus the total ____ W done by the system.
e: Delta U equals net heat into the system minus work done by the system. Q is positive when heat is added, negative when heat is removed. W flips sign if work is done on the system instead.

q: Q is ____ if heat is added to the system, and negative if heat is removed.
e: Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow. Q is if heat is added to cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: W is positive if work is done by the system, and negative if work is done ____ the system.
e: In Delta U = Q - W, W is positive when the system does the work. Work done on the system is negative W in this convention. Heat added is positive Q.

q: The internal energy U of a system is defined as the sum of the energies of all the ____ particles.
e: Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy of the particles. For an ideal gas it depends only on absolute temperature. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work. Internal energy U of a system is cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The internal energy of ideal gases depends only on ____, not on volume or pressure.
e: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, not on volume or pressure. U is proportional to absolute temperature. An isothermal ideal-gas process therefore has Delta U = 0.

q: Note that internal energy of an ideal gas is directly proportional to the ____ temperature.
e: Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy of the particles. For an ideal gas it depends only on absolute temperature. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work. Note that internal energy of an ideal cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Heat transfer and work are both energy in ____.
e: Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow. Heat and work are energy in transit, not stored piles.

q: Internal energy is a form of energy completely different from either heat or ____.
e: In Delta U = Q - W, W is positive when the system does the work. Heat and work are energy in transit, not stored piles. Over a cycle Delta U is zero, so net work equals net heat.

q: A thermodynamic process may be defined as a change from one ____ state of a system to another.
e: A thermodynamic process is a change from one equilibrium state to another. Quasi-static means you crawl slowly enough to stay in internal equilibrium. A sudden bang is not that ideal path.

q: In thermodynamics, a ____ process (also known as a quasi-equilibrium process) is a thermodynamic process that happens slowly enough for the system to remain in internal physical thermodynamic equilibrium.
e: A quasi-static, or quasi-equilibrium, process is slow enough that the system remains in internal thermodynamic equilibrium. You can then draw it as a curve on a p-V diagram and retrace it. Rapid processes jump off that curve.

q: An isobaric process occurs at constant ____.
e: Isobaric means constant pressure. Work done by the system is then p Delta V. Constant volume is isochoric, constant temperature is isothermal.

q: The work done by the system in an isobaric process is simply the pressure multiplied by the change in ____.
e: Isobaric means constant pressure. Work done by the system is then p Delta V. Constant volume is isochoric, constant temperature is isothermal. Work done by the system in an cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: An isochoric process occurs at constant ____.
e: Isochoric means constant volume, so W = p Delta V = 0. First law then says Delta U equals the heat that entered or left. For an ideal gas that heat is n Cv Delta T.

q: When the volume of a thermodynamic system is constant, no ____ is done by the system because $W=p\Delta V=0$.
e: In Delta U = Q - W, W is positive when the system does the work. Heat and work are energy in transit, not stored piles. Over a cycle Delta U is zero, so net work equals net heat. Work done on the system is negative W in this convention.

q: According to the first law, the change in internal energy must equal any ____ flowing into or out of the system.
e: Delta U equals net heat into the system minus work done by the system. Q is positive when heat is added, negative when heat is removed. W flips sign if work is done on the system instead. According to the first law the change cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: An isothermal process occurs at a constant ____ (i.e. $\Delta T=0$).
e: Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium. Isochoric holds V; isobaric holds p; adiabatic holds Q at zero.

q: For a process to be isothermal, any heat flow into or out of the system must occur ____ to maintain the thermodynamic equilibrium of the system.
e: Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium. Isochoric holds V; isobaric holds p; adiabatic holds Q at zero. Work is n R T ln(Vf/Vi) for the ideal-gas case.

q: However, for an ideal gas, internal energy U is only a ____ of the temperature.
e: Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy of the particles. For an ideal gas it depends only on absolute temperature. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work. However for an ideal gas internal energy cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: In an isothermal process internal energy is constant; therefore, $\Delta U$ is equal to ____ for an isothermal process.
e: Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium. Isochoric holds V; isobaric holds p; adiabatic holds Q at zero. Isothermal process internal energy is constant therefore cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: If the system does the work, the energy comes from heat flowing into the system from the ____.
e: Heat is energy flowing because temperatures differ. It is not a stored fluid sitting inside a body. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow. In Delta U = Q - W, W is positive when the system does the work.

q: In an adiabatic process, there is no ____ transfer into or out of the system, i.e. $Q=0$.
e: Adiabatic means Q = 0, no heat in or out, often by insulating the system. First law collapses to Delta U = -W. Isothermal holds T and lets heat leak; adiabatic forbids heat.

q: Heat engine is a system that converts heat to ____ energy, which can then be used to do mechanical work.
e: A heat engine converts heat into mechanical energy so it can do mechanical work. It repeats a cycle so work keeps coming out. Turning work into heat is dissipation, not this engine.

q: A series of processes in which a system is brought back to its initial state is called a ____.
e: A cycle is a series of processes that returns the system to its initial state. Net Delta U over a cycle is zero. Then W equals Q_H minus Q_C for a heat engine.

q: The purpose of a heat engine is to deliver ____ continuously to the outside by performing the same cycle over and over again.
e: In Delta U = Q - W, W is positive when the system does the work. Heat and work are energy in transit, not stored piles. Over a cycle Delta U is zero, so net work equals net heat. A heat engine turns heat from a hot source into mechanical work and dumps leftover heat to a cold sink.

q: Thermal efficiency for a heat engine is the ____ of work output to heat input.
e: Thermal efficiency is work output over heat input, W/Q_H. You can also write 1 - Q_C/Q_H. Heat input over work output is the reciprocal, not the efficiency.

q: The transformation of heat into work is usually accomplished in practice by two general types of engine; the internal ____ engine and the steam engine.
e: Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy of the particles. For an ideal gas it depends only on absolute temperature. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work. A heat engine turns heat from a hot source into mechanical work and dumps leftover heat to a cold sink.

q: In both engines, a gas or a mixture of gases contained in a ____ undergoes a cycle.
e: A heat engine turns heat from a hot source into mechanical work and dumps leftover heat to a cold sink. Efficiency is W over Q_H. A full cycle has net Delta U = 0, so W = Q_H - Q_C.

q: There are two types of internal combustion engine (gasoline engine and diesel engine) that generates the input heat by the ____ of fuel within the engine itself.
e: A gasoline engine intakes fuel plus air and ignites with an electric spark. Four piston motions are the strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Diesel instead intakes air only and auto-ignites injected fuel.

q: In the gasoline engines, the combustion of the gasoline and air takes place explosively by an electric ____.
e: A gasoline engine ignites the fuel-air mix with an electric spark. Four of the six processes are piston strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Diesel instead compresses air only and injects fuel that auto-ignites.

q: The cycle involves the performance of six processes, of which four require motion of the piston and are called ____.
e: Four piston motions in the gasoline cycle are the strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Spark ignition happens between compression and power, at nearly constant volume. Diesel still has strokes but intakes air only.

q: Intake stroke: A mixture of gasoline vapour and air is drawn into the cylinder by the ____ stroke of the piston.
e: On the gasoline intake, or suction, stroke the piston draws in gasoline vapour and air. Diesel intake draws air only. Compression then raises p and T of whatever was drawn in.

q: Compression stroke: The mixture of gasoline vapour and air is ____ until its pressure and temperature rise considerably.
e: The compression stroke squeezes the charge until pressure and temperature rise sharply. Gasoline then waits for a spark; diesel waits for injected fuel. Volume falls; p and T climb.

q: Explosion: Combustion of the hot mixture is caused to take place very ____ by an electric spark.
e: Gasoline combustion is a rapid spark explosion at nearly constant volume; the piston barely moves in that instant. Pressure jumps, then the power stroke expands the hot gases. Diesel ignition is compression heat plus injection, not that spark pop.

q: Power stroke: The hot combustion products ____ and push the piston out, thus suffering a drop in pressure and temperature.
e: On the power stroke the hot gases expand, push the piston, and drop in pressure and temperature. That is the work-delivery leg. Exhaust then dumps what is left.

q: Valve exhaust: The combustion products at the end of the power stroke are still at a ____ pressure and temperature than the outside.
e: On the power stroke the hot gases expand, push the piston, and drop in pressure and temperature. That is the work-delivery leg. Exhaust then dumps what is left. Valve exhaust The combustion products at the cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Exhaust stroke: The piston pushes almost all the remaining combustion products out of the cylinder by exerting a pressure sufficiently ____ than that of the outside pressure.
e: The exhaust stroke has the piston push remaining combustion products out. They still leave hotter and at higher pressure than the outside. A slightly larger push than outside pressure is needed to empty the cylinder.

q: The diesel engine operates on either a two-stroke or four-stroke cycle; however, unlike the spark-ignition gasoline engine, the diesel engine induces only ____ into the combustion chamber on its intake stroke.
e: A gasoline engine ignites the fuel-air mix with an electric spark. Four of the six processes are piston strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Diesel instead compresses air only and injects fuel that auto-ignites. Diesel intake draws air only.

q: Diesel fuel is sprayed into the cylinder by the injector (nozzle) and immediately ____ because of the heat and pressure inside the cylinder.
e: A diesel draws only air, then sprays fuel that ignites from compression heat and pressure. No spark is required at that instant. Two-stroke or four-stroke versions both exist.

q: The pressure created by the combustion of the fuel drives the piston ____.
e: A gas confined by a piston in a cylinder is the usual thermodynamic system. Heat in, work out, and U can all be tracked on that cylinder. Strokes are the piston motions in an engine cycle.

q: In 1824, ____, French engineer, described a hypothetical engine known as Carnot engine.
e: In 1824 Sadi Carnot described a hypothetical reversible engine between two reservoirs. That Carnot engine sets the upper efficiency bound for every real engine on the same pair of temperatures. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow.

q: It is a heat engine operates on an ideal ____ cycle (Carnot cycle) between two heat reservoirs.
e: A reversible process can retrace the same p-V path if you go infinitesimally slowly. Carnot's four legs are all reversible. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow.

q: Carnot engine sets an ____ limit on the efficiency of all other real engines, such as steam engines, gasoline and diesel engines.
e: Heat-engine efficiency is work out divided by heat in, W/Q_H or 1 - Q_C/Q_H. Carnot replaces the heat ratio with T_C/T_H on an absolute scale. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow.

q: All real engines are less efficient than Carnot engine because they do not operate through a reversible cycle, and efficiency is further reduced due to ____ and energy losses by conduction.
e: The Carnot engine runs a reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats between two reservoirs. It is an upper limit, not a workshop motor. Convection and radiation are the other two modes, with bulk flow or electromagnetic waves.

q: In a reversible process, the system undergoing the process can be returned to its initial ____ along the same path on the p-V diagram.
e: In a reversible process you can return along the same p-V path to the start. Infinitesimally slow is the main thermodynamic condition. An irreversible process cannot retrace that path.

q: A process that does not satisfy these requirements is an ____ process.
e: A reversible process can retrace the same p-V path if you go infinitesimally slowly. Carnot's four legs are all reversible. Friction and finite-speed flow make real engines irreversible and less efficient.

q: The most important condition for a process to be reversible in thermodynamics is that the process should be carried out ____ slowly.
e: Thermodynamics maps equilibrium states involving heat and work. Heat transfer then asks how energy actually flows. The two branches complement each other; they are not unrelated. A reversible process can retrace the same p-V path if you go infinitesimally slowly.

q: The working substance of a Carnot engine is an ____ gas contained in a cylinder fitted with a movable piston at one end.
e: Carnot's reversible engine between two reservoirs sets the efficiency ceiling. The cycle is two isotherms and two adiabats. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow.

q: The Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes; two isothermal processes and two ____ processes.
e: Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium. Isochoric holds V; isobaric holds p; adiabatic holds Q at zero. Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Carnot analyzed the transformation of energy during one complete cycle of this engine's performance and determined the conditions for ____ efficiency.
e: A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow.

q: Kelvin proposed that we use a Carnot engine as a ____ and define the ratio of two temperatures as the ratio of the heat absorbed by the engine to the heat rejected.
e: Carnot's reversible engine between two reservoirs sets the efficiency ceiling. The cycle is two isotherms and two adiabats. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow. A full cycle has net Delta U = 0, so W = Q_H - Q_C.

q: Although Carnot engine is not ____ efficient, but it is more efficient than other machine in transforming heat into work.
e: Carnot's reversible engine between two reservoirs sets the efficiency ceiling. The cycle is two isotherms and two adiabats. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow. Efficiency is W over Q_H.

q: ____ theorem states that no engine operating between two heat reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same reservoirs.
e: Carnot's reversible engine between two reservoirs sets the efficiency ceiling. The cycle is two isotherms and two adiabats. Real engines sit below this reversible ceiling because of friction and finite-speed flow. A heat engine turns heat from a hot source into mechanical work and dumps leftover heat to a cold sink.
